column1: Rigorous Cross-Examination of Conflicting Estimates, System Boundary Asymmetries, and Literature Voids [Analytical Inferences Marked [I]]

column2: Global Annual Data Centre Direct Water Consumption
column3: 140 billion L direct water consumption globally in 2023 (P04, EXT-070, pdf p. 5 citing IEA 2024)
column4: >560 billion L in 2024 (P10, EXT-155, pdf p. 3; P07, EXT-195, pdf p. 7 citing IEA 2025)
column5: IEA 2024 estimated 140 billion L direct water on 360 TWh electricity demand (P04, EXT-070, pdf p. 5); Baringa (P10, EXT-155) reports >560 billion L globally in 2024, rising to 1.2 trillion L by 2030.
column6: Top-down global intensity benchmarks severely underestimate real-world evaporative cooling demand by ignoring local climate extremes and peak summer temperatures.

column2: Direct Operational WUEsite Benchmarks Across Facilities
column3: AWS direct site WUE = 0.12 L/kWh, Meta = 0.19 L/kWh, Microsoft = 0.27 L/kWh (P14, PRS-024, pdf p. 2 citing Rystad Energy 2026)
column4: Google average direct WUE = 1.04 L/kWh (P04, EXT-075, pdf p. 7); Equinix direct WUE = 0.91 L/kWh (P14, PRS-024, pdf p. 2)
column5: Conflation of system boundaries (withdrawal vs consumption), distinct climate zones of data centre fleets, and differing cooling architectures (direct evaporative vs chilled water vs air-cooled chillers). Masanet notes studies frequently fail to disclose WUE sources (P06, EXT-129, EXT-130, pdf p. 117).
column6: A single universal WUE benchmark cannot be applied across operators or geographies without adjusting for local wet-bulb temperature, economizer hours, and reporting boundary.

column2: Share of Data Centres Located in Water-Stressed Areas
column3: 20% of US data centre direct water from stressed subbasins (P02, EXT-022, pdf p. 3 using AWARE); 25% of global data centres face water gaps (P05, EXT-082, pdf p. 1)
column4: 32% of US facilities in high/extremely high stress (P09, EXT-147, pdf p. 3; explicitly United States, not global); 41% of Asian data centres in extremely high stress (P08, EXT-182, pdf p. 2); 52% of global hubs in water-stressed regions (P10, EXT-158, pdf p. 3)
column5: Differences in geographic scope (US vs Global vs Asia), differing hydrological stress indices (ISO 14046 AWARE vs monthly water gaps vs WRI Aqueduct BWS), and varying stress thresholds (40% vs 80%).
column6: When evaluated using identical stress metrics, Asian and Indian data centres face nearly double the extreme water stress exposure of North American facilities.

column2: System Boundary Accounting: Water Withdrawal vs. Water Consumption
column3: Consumption (evaporative loss from local watershed) is the essential metric for assessing hydrological resource depletion (P01, EXT-008, pdf p. 1; P02, EXT-026, pdf p. 4; P04, EXT-068, pdf p. 5; P06, EXT-106, pdf p. 1)
column4: Corporate disclosures and utility reporting frequently measure Withdrawal (total water intake, including return flows), which is easier to meter but conflates non-consumptive cooling with net loss (P03, EXT-048, pdf p. 2; P09, EXT-133, pdf p. 2; P14, PRS-024, pdf p. 2)
column5: Operators report withdrawal to align with municipal utility billing meters or claim water circularity, while hydrologists require consumption to evaluate local watershed mass balances.
column6: Conflating withdrawal and consumption distorts water footprint evaluations because withdrawal includes recirculated or returned volumes (P01, pdf p. 1, EXT-008; P06, pdf p. 1, EXT-106). Studies emphasize that consumption (evaporative loss) is the critical parameter for local watershed stress, whereas withdrawal metrics overstate on-site depletion while obscuring actual hydrological balance (P02, pdf p. 4, EXT-026; P06, pdf pp. 1, 18, EXT-106, EXT-116).

column1: 2. SYSTEMATIC LITERATURE GAPS (PAPERS AUDITED ACROSS CORPUS)

column2: Absence of Empirical Facility-Level Water Telemetry in India and Global South
column4: All quantitative facility models are US- or EU-centric; P07 is qualitative/stakeholder-based; P08 is regional text only; no empirical sensor telemetry exists for Indian data centres.
column5: Forces Indian policymakers to rely on unverified corporate CSR claims or imported temperate-climate benchmarks that understate tropical cooling needs.

column2: Omission of Seasonal and Diurnal Hydrological Stress Dynamics
column4: Studies rely on annual baseline stress indices (WRI Aqueduct BWS or annual AWARE); only P05 models monthly water gaps, but no study integrates diurnal peak cooling during summer heatwaves.
column5: In India's monsoon-dependent climate, annual averages mask severe 4-month pre-monsoon water deficits when data centre cooling demand peaks.

column2: Lack of Disaggregation Across Water Source Types (Groundwater vs Municipal vs Tanker)
column4: Corporate disclosures aggregate water into a single volumetric number; only P07 qualitatively notes reliance on private water tankers and borewells in Chennai and Bengaluru.
column5: Prevents direct attribution of data centre cooling to localized groundwater table depletion and aquifer over-extraction in Indian metropolitan fringes.

column2: Total Omission of Scope 3 Embodied Water (Semiconductor Fabrication & Construction)
column4: P03 and P06 explicitly mention Scope 3 embodied water in their conceptual taxonomy (EXT-055, EXT-110), but neither quantifies it; no paper calculates embodied water in chip fabrication.
column5: True lifecycle water footprint of AI expansion is substantially higher than operational metrics reflect, obscuring global water transfer embodied in AI accelerator imports.

column2: Lack of Water Quality and Thermal Discharge Degradation Analysis
column4: Cooling tower blowdown water carries high mineral concentration and biocide chemicals; no paper evaluates downstream ecological or municipal wastewater treatment impacts.
column5: Blowdown discharge in water-scarce Indian cities risks degrading municipal wastewater infrastructure and contaminating surrounding surface water bodies.

column1: 3. WEAKEST POINTS OF EVIDENCE BASE IN CORPUS

column2: Secondary Citation Cascades & Circular Evidence Loops
column3: Multiple studies cite older benchmark figures (e.g. Shehabi et al. 2016 for US totals, or IEA 2024 for global aggregates) rather than generating fresh primary empirical data.
column4: Creates an artificial impression of robust empirical consensus when the entire literature rests on a handful of foundational modeling papers.

column2: Inferential Cooling Technology Modeling Without Ground-Truth Verification
column3: Studies assign cooling systems to facilities via algorithmic proxy (e.g. P05 using climate regression) rather than verified ground-truth data centre equipment registers.
column4: Macro-level regional aggregates are statistically robust, but individual facility allocations carry significant uncertainty.

column2: Complete Opacity of Colocation and Wholesale Data Centres
column3: Colocation facilities host substantial data centre capacity yet disclose virtually zero public water metrics due to multi-tenant split incentives and lack of measurement (P01 notes less than a third of operators measure water consumption, EXT-003, pdf p. 1; P02 notes absence of public commercial facility data, EXT-038, pdf p. 11; P06, EXT-125, pdf p. 48; P07, EXT-205, pdf p. 14).
column4: Literature is heavily skewed toward self-owned hyperscale campuses (Google, Microsoft, Meta), leaving the fastest-growing market segment completely unmonitored.
